Cumulative, beginner-facing, grouped by the week each term is covered (not A–Z). `/course-notes add` appends a `## Week N` section. Never delete an existing entry; a later week may add a stricter-sense note, but the original beginner anchor stays. One sentence plus a cross-reference to the week section that introduces the term.

## Week 1

- **Rule-based software:** a program whose behavior is hand-coded as explicit rules (week 1, Motivation).
- **Machine learning:** programs whose behavior is learned from input–output examples instead of hand-coded (week 1, Motivation).
- **Training set:** a collection of inputs paired with the desired outputs (week 1, Motivation).
- **Feature vector:** the fixed-length vector of measurements $\bm{x}$ describing one input (week 1, Motivation).
- **Deep learning:** models built by composing many small differentiable layers and trained end-to-end with gradient descent (week 1, Motivation).
- **End-to-end learning:** learning the features and the classifier together instead of hand-designing the features (week 1, Motivation).
- **Convex / non-convex loss:** every local minimum of a convex loss is a global minimum, so gradient descent (with a suitable learning rate) can reach one; a non-convex loss can have local optima, saddle points, and flat regions (week 1, Why Deep Learning Was Hard).
- **Linear regression:** a model that predicts a scalar as an affine function of the features, $\hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top\bm{x} + b$ (week 1, Linear Regression).
- **Parameters:** the values $\bm{\theta} = (\bm{w}, b)$ that are tuned and learned from data (week 1, Linear Regression).
- **Loss function:** a measure of how well the model fits the data, used as the objective to minimize (week 1, The loss function).
- **Gradient descent:** repeatedly moving the parameters against the gradient of the loss (week 1, Gradient descent).
- **Learning rate:** the step size $\eta$ of each gradient descent update (week 1, Gradient descent).
- **Chain rule:** the rule for differentiating a composition of functions, used to compute the gradients of the loss (week 1, Computing the gradients).
- **Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent:** updating with the average gradient of a random sample of $B$ examples (week 1, Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent).
- **Hyperparameter:** a setting chosen by the practitioner rather than learned from data (week 1, Hyperparameters).
- **Classification:** predicting a discrete, unordered class label (week 1, Softmax (Logistic) Regression).
- **One-hot vector:** a length-$K$ vector with a 1 at the correct class and 0s elsewhere (week 1, One-hot encoding).
- **Softmax function:** maps class scores to a valid probability distribution (week 1, From scores to probabilities).
- **Cross-entropy loss:** the negative log-likelihood of the true class, with gradient $\hat{\bm{y}} - \bm{y}$ with respect to the scores (week 1, Cross-Entropy Loss).


## Week 2

- **Linear model.** A model whose output changes by the same proportional amount for a given change in an input, everywhere; its graph is a straight line. See [Limitations of Linear Models](lectures/week02.qmd#limitations-of-linear-models).
- **Multi-layer perceptron (MLP).** A model built by stacking linear layers with a nonlinearity between them; also called a feed-forward, fully connected, or dense network. See [The Multi-Layer Perceptron](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-mlp).
- **Activation function.** The elementwise nonlinearity $\sigma$ applied between linear layers. See [Activation Functions](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-activations).
- **Sigmoid, ReLU, tanh.** The three standard activation functions: sigmoid squashes to $(0,1)$, tanh to $(-1,1)$, and ReLU is $\max(0,x)$. See [Activation Functions](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-activations).
- **Pre-activation and activation.** For layer $m$, $a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m$ is the pre-activation and $h^m = \sigma^m(a^m)$ is the activation. See [Backpropagation](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-backprop).
- **Backpropagation.** The algorithm that computes every weight gradient by applying the chain rule from the output layer back to the input, reusing values cached in the forward pass. See [Backpropagation](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-backprop).
- **Vanishing gradients.** Gradients shrinking toward zero in early layers because each backward step multiplies by a small activation derivative (at most 1/4 for sigmoid). See [Backpropagation](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-backprop).
- **Universal Approximation Theorem.** A single-hidden-layer network with enough units can approximate any continuous function on a compact (closed and bounded) domain; it says nothing about how to train or whether it generalizes. See [Universal Approximation Theorem](lectures/week02.qmd#sec-uat).
- **Jacobian matrix.** The matrix of partial derivatives of a layer's outputs with respect to its inputs; the chain rule for vectors multiplies by it (transposed). See [The Backward Recursion](lectures/week02.qmd#the-backward-recursion).
- **Hadamard product ($\odot$).** Entry-by-entry multiplication of two same-shaped arrays; it equals multiplying by a diagonal matrix, which is why elementwise activations use it in backprop. See [The Backward Recursion](lectures/week02.qmd#the-backward-recursion).

## Week 3

- **Pre-activation and activation (Week 3 notation).** Pre-activation is $a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m$ and activation is $h^m = \sigma^m(a^m)$, the same as Week 2. The handwritten Week 3 slides write these as $z^m$ and $a^m$. See [Backprop Revisited](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-backprop-revisited).
- **Sigmoid with cross-entropy.** For a sigmoid output unit and cross-entropy loss, the gradient with respect to the pre-activation simplifies to $h^L - y$. See [Backprop Revisited](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-backprop-revisited).
- **Exploding gradients.** Gradients growing toward infinity as they are propagated backward, the counterpart of vanishing gradients; both come from the repeated matrix multiply and nonlinearity derivative in the backward recursion. See [Vanishing and Exploding Gradients](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-vanishing).
- **Parameter initialization.** The choice of the distribution from which the initial weights are sampled before training. See [Parameter Initialization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-init).
- **Xavier (Glorot) initialization.** Sampling each weight from $\mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \tfrac{2}{n_\text{in} + n_\text{out}}\right)$, a compromise between keeping the forward and backward variances near 1. See [Parameter Initialization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-init).
- **Automatic differentiation (autodiff, autograd).** A system that defines a set of operations and their derivatives and records the operations in a computational graph so gradients can be computed by the chain rule. See [Automatic Differentiation](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-autodiff).
- **Computational graph.** A graph recording a computation, with input (leaf) nodes and one node per operation result. See [Automatic Differentiation](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-autodiff).
- **Validation set.** Held-out labeled examples never used to update the parameters, used to check how well a model generalizes. See [Overfitting](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-overfitting).
- **Overfitting.** Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss stops decreasing and starts to rise. See [Overfitting](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-overfitting).
- **Regularization.** Any change to a training procedure that reduces overfitting. See [Regularization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-regularization).
- **Weight decay.** Adding $\lambda\lVert\bm{w}\rVert_2^2$ to the loss, which turns the gradient step into $(1-2\eta\lambda)\bm{w} - \eta\nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L}$, shrinking the weights each step. See [Regularization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-regularization).
- **Dropout.** Setting each feature to 0 with probability $p$ during training and scaling the others by $1/(1-p)$; at test time the features are used unchanged. See [Regularization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-regularization).
- **Cost of a training step.** Roughly three forward passes, about $3|\theta|$ multiply-adds per example for $|\theta|$ parameters: one for the forward pass, one for the backward recursion, one for the weight gradients. See [The cost of backpropagation](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-cost).
- **He initialization.** The ReLU variant of Xavier initialization, sampling weights with $\sigma = \sqrt{2/n_\text{in}}$. See [Parameter Initialization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-init).
- **Frobenius norm.** The square root of the sum of the squares of all entries of a matrix; weight decay on a matrix penalizes its square, $\lVert W\rVert_F^2$. See [Regularization](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-regularization).
- **Reverse topological order.** Visiting the nodes of a computational graph so that each node comes only after every node that uses it, the order of the autodiff backward pass. See [Automatic Differentiation](lectures/week03.qmd#sec-autodiff).

## Week 4

- **Taylor series.** Writing a function's value at a nearby point $\theta + e$ as a sum of its derivatives at $\theta$; keeping the first two terms gives the first-order (tangent-line) approximation that justifies gradient descent. See [Why Gradient Descent Works](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-taylor).
- **Big-O notation, $O(\epsilon^2)$.** A term that shrinks at least as fast as $\epsilon^2$ when $\epsilon$ is small; used to collect the Taylor terms we drop. See [Why Gradient Descent Works](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-taylor).
- **Divergence.** Steps that move the parameters further from the minimum and raise the loss, typically because the learning rate is too large for the tangent-line approximation to hold. See [Choosing the Learning Rate](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-learning-rate).
- **Batch (full-batch) gradient descent.** Gradient descent using the average gradient over the entire training set at every step; not to be confused with the everyday use of "batch" for a mini-batch. See [Stochastic Gradient Descent](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-sgd).
- **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), strict sense.** Updating with the gradient of one training example drawn uniformly at random; its expected gradient equals the full-batch gradient. In common usage "SGD" also covers the mini-batch version from Week 1. See [Stochastic Gradient Descent](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-sgd).
- **Learning rate schedule.** A rule $\eta(t)$ giving the learning rate at iteration $t$, such as constant, piecewise constant, or exponential decay $\eta_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. See [Learning rate schedules](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-schedules).
- **Implicit regularization.** A reduction in overfitting that comes from the training procedure itself, such as the noise in SGD, rather than from an explicit penalty. See [Choosing the batch size](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-sgd-noise).
- **Curvature.** How quickly the slope of the loss changes in a given direction; steep (high-curvature) directions need small learning rates, gradual (low-curvature) ones make slow progress with them. See [One Learning Rate for Every Parameter?](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-one-eta).
- **Adaptive gradient method.** An optimizer that gives each parameter its own effective learning rate, computed from that parameter's gradient history. See [Momentum](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-momentum).
- **Momentum.** An optimizer that steps along an accumulated gradient $\bm{v}_t = \beta\bm{v}_{t-1} + \bm{g}_t$, so consistent gradients build up larger steps and inconsistent ones cancel. See [Momentum](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-momentum).
- **Exponential moving average.** An average updated as $v_t = \beta v_{t-1} + (1-\beta) g_t$, in which older values count for less; $\beta$ near 1 means a longer effective history. See [Adam](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-adam).
- **First and second moment estimates.** Adam's moving averages of the gradient ($\bm{v}_t$) and of the squared gradient ($\bm{s}_t$), named after the mean and the mean of the square of a distribution. See [Adam](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-adam).
- **Bias correction.** Dividing Adam's accumulators by $1-\beta_1^t$ and $1-\beta_2^t$ to undo their pull toward zero from starting at zero; "bias" here means systematic error in an estimate, not a bias parameter. See [The bias toward zero](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-bias-correction).
- **Adam.** The default optimizer for neural networks: it steps along the bias-corrected average gradient divided by the square root of the bias-corrected average squared gradient, with defaults $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\eta = 0.001$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$. See [The full algorithm](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-adam-algorithm).
- **RMSProp.** An earlier adaptive optimizer resembling Adam, but using the raw gradient in the numerator and no bias correction. See [Other optimizers](lectures/week04.qmd#sec-adam).

## Week 5

- **Inductive bias.** The assumptions built into a model's design that make it prefer some solutions before seeing data; "bias" here is a preference, not a bias parameter. See [Convolutional Neural Networks](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-cnn).
- **Translation invariance (lecture sense) and locality.** The two assumptions behind the convolution: apply the same operation at every position, and look at only a small window. See [From a dense layer to a convolution](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-derive-conv).
- **Convolution layer.** A layer that slides a shared kernel over the input and adds a bias to the dot product at each position; it is a dense layer with sparse, shared weights. See [From a dense layer to a convolution](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-derive-conv).
- **Kernel (filter).** The small grid of shared weights a convolution slides over its input; its dot product with a window measures how much the window looks like the kernel. See [Reading the kernel as a template](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-template).
- **Frobenius inner product.** For two matrices of the same shape, the sum of the products of matching entries, $\langle \bm{V}, \bm{W} \rangle_F = \sum_{a,b} V_{a,b} W_{a,b}$; equal to the ordinary dot product of the two matrices flattened into vectors. A convolution output is the bias plus this inner product of the kernel with a window. See [Reading the kernel as a template](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-template).
- **Feature map.** The output grid of a convolution for one kernel, recording where the kernel's pattern was found. See [From a dense layer to a convolution](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-derive-conv).
- **Parameter sharing.** Reusing one kernel at every position instead of learning separate weights per position. See [From a dense layer to a convolution](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-derive-conv).
- **Cross-correlation versus convolution.** Deep learning's "convolution" lays the kernel over the window as is (cross-correlation); the traditional convolution flips the kernel top-to-bottom and left-to-right first. See [Convolution or cross-correlation?](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-flip).
- **Output-size rule.** Along each axis, $\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$ outputs for input length $n$, kernel $k$, padding $p$ per edge, and stride $s$. See [The general output-size rule](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-general-size).
- **Receptive field.** The region of the input an output entry depends on; through a stack of layers it grows as $r \leftarrow r + (k-1)j$, with jump $j \leftarrow js$. See [Receptive fields of stacked layers](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-rf-stack).
- **Padding.** A border of zeros added before a convolution, usually $\tfrac{K-1}{2}$ per edge so the output keeps the input's size. See [Padding](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-padding).
- **Stride.** How many pixels the window moves between consecutive outputs; PyTorch writes it as (height, width). See [Stride](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-stride).
- **Convolution as a matrix.** Writing a convolution as $\bm{W}\bm{x}$ on the flattened image, where $\bm{W}$ is sparse and repeats the kernel's weights along each row (a Toeplitz-like structure). See [Convolution as a matrix](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-conv-matrix).
- **Channel.** One grid in a stack of same-sized grids, such as the red, green, and blue of a colour image, or one feature map of a layer. See [Channels](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-channels).
- **Convolution parameter count.** $k_h k_w C_\text{in} C_\text{out}$ weights and $C_\text{out}$ biases, independent of the image size. See [Counting parameters](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-param-count).
- **Pooling (max, average).** A parameter-free layer that reduces each window of each channel to one number, usually with stride equal to the window. See [Pooling](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-pooling).
- **Translation equivariance (strict sense).** Shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount, which a convolution satisfies; strict translation *invariance* means the output does not change at all, which pooling provides approximately. See [Invariance and equivariance](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-equivariance).
- **Flatten.** Reshaping an $H\times W\times C$ volume into a vector of $HWC$ entries for a dense layer. See [Building a simple convolutional network](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-simple-convnet).
- **Channels-first layout.** PyTorch's `(N, C, H, W)` ordering of an image batch, versus the lecture's $B\times H\times W\times C$. See [Building a simple convolutional network](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-simple-convnet).
- **Batch normalization.** A layer that standardizes activations with the current mini-batch's mean and variance (per channel for images), then applies a learned scale $\bm{\gamma}$ and shift $\bm{\beta}$. See [Batch Normalization](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-batchnorm).
- **Running statistics.** Batch norm's moving averages of the batch mean and variance, used in place of batch statistics at inference (`model.eval()` in PyTorch). See [How it works](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-batchnorm-how).
- **Internal covariate shift.** The drift in a layer's input distribution as earlier layers train; the original motivation for batch norm, now on uncertain ground. See [Why it might help](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-batchnorm-why).
- **Layer normalization (preview).** Normalizing across the features of a single example rather than across the batch, so each example's output does not depend on the others. See [The trouble with batch normalization](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-batchnorm-trouble).
- **Residual (skip) connection.** Computing $f(\bm{x}) + \bm{x}$ instead of $f(\bm{x})$, giving gradients a path that skips the layer. See [Residual Connections](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-residual).
- **Residual stream.** The running sum carried through a sequence of residual blocks, each adding to it. See [Residual Connections](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-residual).
- **1×1 convolution.** A convolution with a single-position kernel; it changes the number of channels (and, with a stride, downsamples) without looking at neighbours. See [Matching shapes](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-residual-shapes).
- **ResNet.** A convolutional network of stacked residual blocks (conv, BN, ReLU, conv, BN, add, ReLU) between a large input convolution and a global-average-pooling classifier. See [Modern ConvNets: The ResNet](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-resnet).
- **Global average pooling.** Averaging each channel over its whole height and width, turning an $H\times W\times C$ volume into $C$ numbers. See [Modern ConvNets: The ResNet](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-resnet).
- **Data augmentation.** Training on randomly altered copies of examples that keep the same label, such as flips and shifted crops; a form of regularization. See [Preparing Image Data](lectures/week05.qmd#sec-data-prep).

## Week 6

- **Sequence.** An ordered series of random variables $\bm{x}_1, \dots, \bm{x}_T$, where the order dictates a dependency between the elements, as with measurements over time. See [Sequences](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-sequences).
- **Chain rule of probability.** Writing a joint distribution as a product of conditionals, $p(\bm{x}_1)\,p(\bm{x}_2 \mid \bm{x}_1)\cdots p(\bm{x}_T \mid \bm{x}_{T-1}, \dots, \bm{x}_1)$; a different rule from the calculus chain rule of Week 1, which shares only the name. See [Prerequisite: conditional probability and the chain rule of probability](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-chain-rule-prob).
- **Autoregressive sampling.** Generating a sequence one element at a time, feeding each sampled element back in to get the distribution over the next. See [Autoregressive sampling](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-autoregressive).
- **Generative model.** A model of a distribution over data that can be sampled to produce new examples, rather than a predictor of $\bm{y}$ from $\bm{x}$. See [Autoregressive sampling](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-autoregressive).
- **Tokenizer, vocabulary, token.** A tokenizer maps text to integers using a fixed vocabulary $V$ of units (such as words); each unit's integer index is its token, and $|V|$ is the vocabulary size. See [Tokens and one-hot vectors](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-tokens).
- **One-hot vector (input sense).** In Week 1 a one-hot vector encoded a class label; from Week 6 it also encodes an input token, a length-$|V|$ vector with a 1 at the token's index. See [Tokens and one-hot vectors](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-tokens).
- **Embedding matrix and word (token) embedding.** A learned weight matrix with one column per vocabulary entry; multiplying it by a token's one-hot vector selects that token's column, its embedding. See [Embeddings](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-embeddings).
- **Recurrent neural network (RNN), vanilla.** A network that updates a hidden state $\bm{h}_t = \sigma(\bm{W}_x \bm{x}_t + \bm{W}_h \bm{h}_{t-1} + \bm{b}_h)$ at each step and reuses the same weights at every step, so it reads any length with a fixed number of parameters. See [The Vanilla Recurrent Neural Network](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-vanilla-rnn).
- **Hidden state.** The vector $\bm{h}_t$ an RNN carries from step to step, holding information about every input so far. See [The Vanilla Recurrent Neural Network](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-vanilla-rnn).
- **Recurrent connection.** The term $\bm{W}_h \bm{h}_{t-1}$ that feeds the previous hidden state into the current one through a learned matrix $\bm{W}_h$. See [The Vanilla Recurrent Neural Network](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-vanilla-rnn).
- **Unrolling.** Drawing a recurrent network as one copy of its layer per step, all sharing weights, so it can be treated as a deep feed-forward network. See [Backpropagation Through Time](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-bptt).
- **Backpropagation through time (BPTT).** Backpropagation applied to the unrolled recurrent network. See [Backpropagation Through Time](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-bptt).
- **Partial versus total derivative.** A partial derivative holds every other argument fixed; a total derivative counts every path by which the variable affects the result, summing them. See [Prerequisite: total versus partial derivatives](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-total-partial).
- **Exploding and vanishing gradients (recurrent sense).** In an RNN the gradient contains powers of the one recurrent matrix $\bm{W}_h$, so its eigenvalues directly decide whether contributions from far-back steps blow up or fade, making the Week 3 problem more severe. See [Why recurrent networks are hard to train](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-exploding-vanishing).
- **Long short-term memory (LSTM).** A recurrent network with a separate cell state $\bm{c}_t$ whose reading, writing, and forgetting are controlled by gates; it trains more reliably than a vanilla RNN. See [Long Short-Term Memory](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-lstm).
- **Gate.** A vector of values in $(0, 1)$, computed with a sigmoid, that multiplies another vector entry by entry to let each entry through, block it, or pass part of it. See [Long Short-Term Memory](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-lstm).
- **Input, forget, and output gates; candidate cell.** The forget gate scales the old cell, the input gate scales the candidate cell $\tilde{\bm{c}}_t$ (computed with tanh from the current input), and the output gate scales the tanh of the new cell to give $\bm{h}_t$. In the LSTM, $\bm{o}_t$ is the output gate, not the output scores. See [Long Short-Term Memory](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-lstm).
- **Deep RNN.** Stacked recurrent layers, each taking the hidden state of the layer below at the same step as its input. See [Deep RNNs](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-deep-rnn).
- **Bidirectional RNN.** A forward and a backward recurrent layer with separate parameters whose states are concatenated at each step; usable only when the whole sequence is available. See [Bidirectional RNNs](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-bidirectional).
- **Language model.** A model of $p(\bm{x}_t \mid \bm{x}_{t-1}, \dots, \bm{x}_1)$ for text, used to generate text and to score how probable a sequence is. See [Language modeling](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-language-modeling).
- **Teacher forcing.** Training a sequence model by always feeding the true prefix, not the model's own earlier predictions. See [Language modeling](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-language-modeling).
- **Sequence classification.** Predicting one class from a whole sequence, typically from the final hidden state $\bm{h}_T$. See [Sequence classification](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-sequence-classification).
- **Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq), encoder-decoder.** Generating an output sequence conditioned on an input sequence: an encoder RNN reads the input, its final state is the context $\bm{c}$, and a decoder RNN generates the output autoregressively from $\bm{c}$. The context $\bm{c}$ is not the LSTM cell $\bm{c}_t$. See [Sequence-to-Sequence Learning](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-seq2seq).
- **Initial hidden state $\bm{h}_0$.** Usually all zeros or a learned vector; a seq2seq decoder can start from the context instead. See [Sequence-to-Sequence Learning](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-seq2seq).
- **Beginning- and end-of-sequence tokens (`<bos>`, `<eos>`).** Special vocabulary entries that tell the decoder to start generating and signal that the output is finished. See [Sequence-to-Sequence Learning](lectures/week06.qmd#sec-seq2seq).
